content: The study evaluated AxSYM-positive sera using the Monolisa Plus assay, confirming results with immunoblot (IB) per CDC guidelines or PCR. The research assessed the effectiveness of using AxSYM as a screening test and Monolisa Plus as a confirmatory assay in routine clinical laboratories. It concluded that Monolisa Plus could serve as an alternative to immunoblot for confirming AxSYM-positive sera in non-immunocompromised individuals. Barreto et al. conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis comparing three testing strategies, including two CDC-recommended algorithms and the Brazilian national algorithm for diagnosing HCV infection. The cost of each algorithm depended on the number of supplemental tests required. Algorithm A and B (CDC) and Algorithm C (Brazil) were evaluated based on the signal-to-cutoff (s/co) ratio of ELISA anti-HCV samples, with ≥95% concordance with IB positivity. Krajden (2000) described the strengths and limitations of serological and molecular tests for diagnosing hepatitis C. Serological tests detect antibodies to HCV, while molecular tests detect or quantify HCV RNA. The combination of an antibody test followed by a confirmatory nucleic acid test (NAT) is widely accepted. Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) for HCV antibody detection are simple, inexpensive, and time-efficient but cannot distinguish between acute, active, or chronic non-viremic HCV infections. EIA sensitivity is 97–99% in chronically infected individuals but drops to 50–70% in acutely infected individuals. Rapid antibody tests are more expensive and less suitable for high-volume testing but can be cost-effective in low-volume or field settings. NAT remains the gold standard for identifying active infection, detecting HCV RNA as early as one week post-exposure. However, NAT is costly, requires skilled technicians, and demands robust infrastructure. NAT methods include PCR, branched DNA signal amplification, and transcription-mediated amplification, with specificities up to 99% across all six HCV genotypes. HCV core antigen testing has emerged as a commercially available alternative. Tillmann (2014) highlighted its potential as a serological test for identifying active infection and as a possible replacement for NAT in confirmatory testing. While less sensitive than HCV RNA tests, core antigen testing is cost-effective and can be integrated into existing platforms. Cresswell (2014) demonstrated its efficacy and cost-effectiveness in diagnosing acute HCV in high-risk populations, such as HIV-positive MSM. Core antigen testing is a quick, simple, and cost-effective screening tool for acute HCV in high-prevalence settings. Other testing options include recombinant immunoblot tests, signal-to-cutoff ratios, and point-of-care tests (POCTs) or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Immunoblots are highly specific but technically complex, costly, and time-consuming, making them unsuitable for routine use. Signal-to-cutoff ratios, while useful for reducing supplemental testing, require skilled interpretation and are better suited for high-throughput clinical laboratories. Shivkumar (2012) conducted a meta-analysis on the diagnostic accuracy of POCTs and RDTs for HCV screening, finding that blood-based POCTs had the highest accuracy, followed by serum/plasma RDTs and oral fluid POCTs. More evidence is needed to incorporate these newer tests into diagnostic algorithms. CDC guidelines recommend an anti-HCV test followed by a sensitive HCV RNA test to confirm active infection. FDA-approved tests, such as the OraQuick HCV rapid antibody test, are recommended for screening. For individuals positive for anti-HCV but negative for HCV RNA, no further testing is needed unless there is suspicion of recent infection, in which case repeat HCV RNA testing is advised. To differentiate between resolved remote infection and false-positive results, a second FDA-approved HCV antibody test using a different assay is recommended. Studies have shown that using a highly sensitive EIA followed by another EIA as a confirmatory test is effective in non-immunocompromised populations. However, immunoblot assays remain more effective in immunocompromised patients due to their lower antibody levels. Cost-effective algorithms, such as using a sensitive test for initial screening followed by a second test to confirm viremia, have been demonstrated in settings like Cameroon.
